title: Event Management — The School Event Challenge
subject: Skill Education

blocks.text: EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 1  UNDERSTAND THE EVENT BRIEF
Mission 1 • Ask first • Check the setting • Suggested learning time 3 hours

The school says, “Please organise a project showcase.” One teammate starts designing a poster, while another wants a large stage. But who is the event for, what should visitors experience, and what has the school agreed? Your first task is to turn the request into a clear, realistic brief.
THINK  Which unanswered question could make the team’s first plan unrealistic?
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN

Clarify the purpose, intended audience, expected outcome and limits of a proposed school event. Consult the responsible school adult, inspect the proposed venue and produce a reviewed event brief. Mark unanswered questions as pending.
WHAT YOU NEED

Paper, pencil, clipboard, the school’s event request if available, a ruler or tape only if authorised, and access to a teacher-arranged conversation and venue visit. A phone, computer and printing are optional.
LET US UNDERSTAND

An event brief is a shared starting agreement: why the event matters, who it serves, what it includes and which limits apply. It is not the detailed budget, final layout or permission to begin every task. Those decisions develop through later activities.
OUR PRACTICAL TASK

Each student asks or checks at least one question, records one venue observation and contributes to the brief. Use temporary interviewer, observer, note-taker and checker roles; the formal event team is developed in Activity 3.
SAFE START  No bookings, purchases, invitations, furniture moves or electrical tests in this activity. Teacher approval is required for site access and every later commitment.

START HERE  Read the school’s actual request. Prepare questions about purpose, audience, time, venue and limits before consulting staff. CHECK BEFORE MOVING ON  Your brief separates confirmed decisions from pending ones; it does not invent an event detail.
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
READ THE REQUEST  CHECK THE REALITY
A request becomes a workable brief when its limits are clear
ASK ABOUT
WHAT WE NEED TO KNOW
Purpose and outcome
What should participants or visitors learn, see or do? What would a successful event look like?
Audience and scale
Who is expected? What approximate number is the school considering? What needs must we check in Activity 2?
Date and duration
Which date window, setup time and event duration are possible? What clashes must be checked?
Venue and access
Which space is proposed? What routes, facilities and access needs require adult review?
Resources and money
What can be reused or borrowed? What spending limit and purchasing rules apply?
Responsibilities and approvals
Who is the school organiser? Who approves scope, venue, costs, communication and safety?
THINK  If the school has not confirmed a spending limit, how should it appear in your brief?
LET US EXPLORE THE PROPOSED VENUE

Walk the teacher-approved route with a school adult. Observe the room’s existing use, entrances, visible paths and available display surfaces. Note what you saw and what must be checked. Do not infer a safe visitor capacity from a sketch or floor area; the school decides it.
One question for the school organiser or caretaker: __________________________________________________
EXAMPLE ONLY  A SMALL CLASSROOM SHOWCASE

Purpose: share class projects with a teacher-approved group. Possible venue: an existing classroom, subject to school checks. Date, visitor numbers and costs: pending organiser confirmation. First evidence needed: a venue visit and a discussion of scope. This example is not your school’s approved brief.

COMMUNITY AND WORK CONNECTION  A school organiser, caretaker or support staff member can explain how events fit real school routines. Ask about their work respectfully and record how their advice changes your plan.
THINK  Which detail in your brief still needs a named checker?
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 1  FIVE INVESTIGATION STEPS
Read → visit → consult → write → review
1  READ THE REQUEST AND PREPARE QUESTIONS  |  25 MIN

With the teacher, choose one possible event. State the request in your own words. Agree temporary roles and list the important unanswered questions from page 85. Each student prepares a question or a check.
2  INSPECT THE PROPOSED VENUE  |  30 MIN

Visit with the school adult. Record what is visible and the current use of the space. Sketch an observation, not a final layout. Keep routes clear and do not move equipment. Separate observed facts from assumptions and questions for later checking.
3  CONSULT THE SCHOOL ORGANISER  |  35 MIN

Ask the teacher, event coordinator or nominated staff member about purpose, audience, dates, scale, resources and approvals. Each student contributes. Record the person’s role, date, advice and pending decisions. Check your understanding back with them.
4  WRITE THE EVENT BRIEF  |  35 MIN

Complete page 87 using the request, venue observation and staff advice. Describe a manageable outcome and school limits. Use “pending” for an unconfirmed date, cost or visitor number. Do not invent a commitment to fill a box.
5  PEER CHECK AND REVISE  |  35 MIN

Swap briefs with another team. Can they explain the purpose and identify the limits? Revise one unclear or unrealistic point. Present the brief to the teacher and record the review decision on page 89. Explain each student’s contribution.
THINK  Two teams interpret the same request differently. What evidence could help them agree on the scope?
FINAL 20 MIN  REFLECT AND RECEIVE FEEDBACK

Complete the five questions on page 88. Review the brief and next questions with the teacher. Total suggested learning time: 180 minutes. Arrange the conversation and venue visit within the school timetable.
DIGITAL CHECK  If notes are typed or shared, use approved school storage. Record sources and dates. Do not publish an unapproved event date or invitation while the brief is still under review.
THINK  Which venue observation should appear in your brief?

Keep the original request and your first version where available. A reviewed brief can change later, but record the change and obtain the relevant approval before acting.
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 1  THINK AND REFLECT
Five questions • Explain how your investigation improved the brief
1. What is the purpose of your proposed event, and what should visitors or participants gain from it?
2. Which venue observation or staff explanation changed your first idea? Refer to a real note or date.
3. Why must an unconfirmed spending limit, visitor number or event date stay marked as pending?
4. What useful question did you ask or check, and how did it help your team make the brief clearer?
5. What can the team do next with the reviewed brief, and which actions still require specific school approval?
WHAT DID WE LEARN

A workable event starts with questions, real observations and shared understanding. A brief connects purpose, people, place, time and resources. Recording a pending decision is more useful than pretending it has been approved.
CONNECT WITH PEOPLE AND HOME
A school worker’s role I understand better: __________________________________________________
A question I would ask before helping with a small home occasion: __________________________________________________

ACTIVITY 1  OUR REVIEWED EVENT BRIEF
A clear starting agreement • A record of checks • A realistic next step
SHOW THE SETTING WE CHECKED
Draw or attach a permitted sketch/photo of the proposed space. Label one observed feature and one pending check. This is not the final venue layout.
OUR VENUE OBSERVATION
THINK  What makes this brief ready for visitor research even if some decisions are still pending?
EVIDENCE OF LEARNING

□ Request understood  □ Staff conversation and venue observation recorded □ Brief completed with uncertainties marked  □ Peer check and revision shown □ Individual contribution recorded  □ Teacher review and next questions noted
TEACHER FEEDBACK  ACTIVITY 1
I = independently, P = with a prompt, N = needs practice. Observe each student’s investigation and explanation, not just the team’s finished sheet.
AREA
OBSERVABLE EVIDENCE
I / P / N
Practical
Asks/checks a question, observes the venue and records a coherent brief.
Work
Uses school-worker advice to clarify realistic event requirements.
Values
Shares investigation roles and distinguishes agreements from assumptions.
Home
Explains a useful planning question for a small home occasion.
Teacher decision: ready for next inquiry / revise / await key decision: __________________________________________________
Outstanding question / responsible adult / next review date: __________________________________________________
Review of the brief is not blanket permission to spend, invite, book or run the event. Retain the school’s normal approval steps as later plans develop.
NEXT  Activity 2 — Know Your Visitors. Investigate the needs of the intended audience before fixing the visitor experience.
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 2  KNOW YOUR VISITORS
Listen to real people • Find needs • Make useful recommendations
AI-generated illustrative photograph. Your evidence must come from your own supervised visitor inquiry.
THINK  What might a visitor need that our event team has not thought of yet?
OUR LEARNING OBJECTIVE
We will ask respectful questions, record real responses and use the evidence to recommend a more welcoming event.
TIME AND WHAT YOU NEED

150 minutes of instructional time across scheduled sessions. Bring the reviewed Activity 1 brief, reused paper, pencil, clipboard or firm book, and a teacher-approved question sheet. A device is optional.
LET US UNDERSTAND
An event works better when its visitors can find their way, understand what is happening and take part. People of the same age may have different needs. Ask and check instead of guessing.

START HERE  Find the intended audience in your brief. Practise your questions, then consult the teacher-approved visitors. CHECK BEFORE MOVING ON  Each recommendation points to a real anonymous response; note whose views are missing.
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
EXPLORE WHO MAY VISIT
Start with the audience in your reviewed event brief
LOOK BACK BEFORE YOU ASK
Read the audience, scale and pending decisions on page 87. Keep the event purpose and school limits. If the audience is still uncertain, ask the organiser which group you may consult first.
VISITOR GROUP TO CHECK
WHAT WE NEED TO FIND OUT
Younger or same-age students
What interests them? What instructions or explanations help?
Parents or community visitors, if invited
What do they need to know before arriving?
People needing a different way to participate
What route, seating, language or communication support would help?
Staff who welcome or guide visitors
What questions do visitors commonly ask?
THINK  Which intended visitor group would our easiest-to-reach sample leave out?
OUR INQUIRY PLAN
Event / intended audience from the brief
People or groups to approach / why these voices matter
Teacher-approved location, time and supervising adult
A group we cannot consult yet / how we will flag the gap
A small inquiry informs planning; it does not represent every visitor. Aim for 4–6 short conversations per team, adjusted by the teacher. Include more than one relevant viewpoint where possible.

COMMUNITY CONNECTION  If community visitors are intended, the teacher can arrange a school-based conversation with a parent representative or school worker. Students do not contact strangers independently.
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
MAKE QUESTIONS THAT HELP
Prepare • Try • Improve
OUR SHORT QUESTION SHEET
Use these open questions as a starting point. Adapt the wording to your real event and visitor group. Ask one question at a time and allow the person to skip any question.
ASK
LISTEN FOR
1 What would you most like to see or do at this event?
An interest linked to the event purpose
2 What information would help you before you arrive?
Timing, place, route or language needs
3 What could make it difficult for you to take part?
A barrier the person chooses to describe
4 What would help you find your way or understand a display?
A practical support or clearer explanation
5 Is there one other thing our team should consider?
An idea our questions missed
THINK  How could “You will enjoy our science games, won’t you?” influence the answer?
TRY THE QUESTIONS WITH A CLASSMATE
One person asks; one answers as themselves; one checks clarity. Rotate. Do not count this practice as a real visitor response unless that student is also an intended visitor and freely agrees.
A question that confused our partner / our clearer version
ASK PERMISSION IN SIMPLE WORDS
“We are planning a school event with our teacher. May we ask a few short questions to improve it? You may skip a question or stop. We will record anonymous notes for our class project.”

RESPECT AND PRIVACY  Follow the school’s permission arrangements. Record visitor codes V1, V2 and so on, not names, phone numbers or medical details. Do not take photos, audio or video without school approval and the required permission. Keep notes in teacher-approved storage.
THINK  Could another student trace your recommendation to a visitor response?
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
DO THE VISITOR INQUIRY
150 minutes • Practical work shared by every student
1 CHECK THE BRIEF AND PLAN  |  15 MIN
Use page 91 to agree whom to consult, where and when. Get the teacher’s agreement before approaching anyone. Do not change the event scope on your own.
2 PREPARE AND PILOT QUESTIONS  |  25 MIN
Use page 92. Try the questions with a classmate, remove leading wording and choose an accessible way to respond: speaking, writing, pointing or a supported response.
3 LISTEN TO REAL VISITORS  |  40 MIN

Work in supervised pairs or small teams. Rotate questioner, listener/recorder and checker roles so everyone practises. Ask permission, listen without interrupting, check your understanding and thank the person. Record notes on page 94.
4 COMPARE EVIDENCE AND PROPOSE CHANGES  |  30 MIN

Group similar responses. Count how many people mentioned each need, without counting the same person twice for that need. Keep an unusual access need visible even if only one person mentioned it. Complete page 95.
5 SHARE AND RECEIVE FEEDBACK  |  20 MIN

Explain one recommendation and its evidence to another team and the teacher. Record feedback. Mark ideas as proposed, accepted for later planning or needing a check. This is not permission to buy, publish or invite.
6 REFLECT AND DOCUMENT  |  20 MIN
Answer the five questions on page 96. Check that original notes, tallies, recommendations and individual contributions can be traced. Record what still needs inquiry.
THINK  If only one person identifies a participation barrier, should we ignore it because most people did not mention it?

FIELDWORK CARE  Stay within the approved school area and supervision. Keep routes clear. Never test a barrier by restricting someone’s movement or simulating a disability. Ask what would help and let the teacher check feasibility.
THINK  Which question did you improve after trying it?

LOGBOOK 2  LISTENING RECORD
Anonymous notes • Actual words or honest paraphrases
CODE / VISITOR GROUP
WHAT THEY SAID OR NEEDED
OUR CHECK OR FOLLOW-UP

Use a visitor group only if relevant and freely shared. Copy this sheet if needed. Label exact words with quotation marks; otherwise write “summary”. If the person declined, record no response rather than inventing one.

Something we checked by asking “Have we understood correctly?”
My question / listening / recording contribution
Total people who responded / groups not yet heard

TURN VOICES INTO ACTION
Evidence → Need → Proposed response → Check
Total respondents: ______. A person may mention several needs, so category totals may exceed the number of respondents. A tally describes this small sample only.
NEED / CODES
NUMBER OF PEOPLE
OUR PROPOSED RESPONSE / CHECK
THINK  Which recommendation could help visitors using materials the school already has?
CHOOSE TWO RECOMMENDATIONS
1 Our recommendation / supporting visitor code(s) / reason
2 Our recommendation / supporting visitor code(s) / reason

Possible responses include clearer reusable signs, a shorter explanation or seating at a display. These are examples, not findings. Check the real need, venue limits, cost and staff advice before deciding.
REVIEW WITH THE TEACHER
Feedback / change made / issue requiring a further check
Decision: proposed / carry into later planning / investigate further Responsible person / next check date: ___________________________________
WHAT DID WE LEARN?  Listening turns a general audience description into practical requirements. Evidence can justify a change, while missing voices and uncertain details show what to check next.

ACTIVITY 2  THINK AND REFLECT
Use your own notes and practical experience
1 What did a real visitor tell you that surprised your team?
2 Which question did you improve after the practice conversation, and why?
3 Which recommendation has the clearest evidence? Refer to visitor codes.
4 Whose views are missing, and how might that affect your conclusions?
5 How did you help someone feel heard, and where could this skill help at home?
EVIDENCE OF LEARNING

□ Inquiry plan and revised questions   □ Anonymous original notes □ Counts linked to visitor codes   □ Two evidence-based recommendations □ Teacher feedback and revision   □ Individual contribution and reflection
TEACHER FEEDBACK
Observe each student, not only the team sheet. I = independently; P = with a prompt; N = needs practice.
AREA
OBSERVABLE EVIDENCE
I / P / N
Practical
Asks a clear question and records a faithful response.
Work
Uses visitor or staff advice to propose a feasible service change.
Values
Listens respectfully, shares turns and protects privacy.
Home
Explains a useful application of listening at home.
NEXT  Activity 3 — Build the Event Team. Carry the reviewed brief and visitor requirements into the responsibility plan.
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 3  BUILD THE EVENT TEAM
Agree the work • Share responsibility • Practise a handover
AI-generated illustrative photograph. Build your own team records for the real school event.
THINK  If everybody says “we will do it”, how will we know who checks that it is done?
OUR LEARNING OBJECTIVE
We will turn the event brief and visitor needs into clear tasks, agree fair roles and test whether another person can continue our work from a handover.
TIME AND WHAT YOU NEED

150 instructional minutes. Bring the reviewed brief on page 87, visitor recommendations on page 95, reused paper, pencils, a clipboard and a school-approved display space. Tape or reusable clips are optional. No device or purchase is required.
LET US UNDERSTAND

A role is useful when its work, deadline and evidence are clear. A student coordinator helps people communicate; the teacher remains responsible for school approvals and supervision. A small event may combine roles.

START HERE  List actual event tasks before choosing role titles. Accept one task and explain its output to your backup. CHECK BEFORE MOVING ON  Your partner can continue a real task using your handover; record what happened.
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
EXPLORE THE WORK BEFORE THE TITLES
Use the real brief and visitor evidence
FIRST ASK WHAT NEEDS TO HAPPEN
Read the approved purpose and limits. Choose tasks needed for your event; do not copy every example. Keep later planning decisions open until their activities are completed.
WORK AREA
POSSIBLE TASK / EVIDENCE
Coordination
Keep the shared task list current; check unresolved decisions with the teacher.
Venue and displays
Prepare a draft layout and list existing resources for later review.
Time and resources
Prepare a draft timetable and cost record; teacher authorises spending.
Communication
Draft clear invitations and reusable signs; teacher reviews before release.
Visitor services
Prepare the registration and help desk plan using visitor needs.
Readiness and records
Track checks, feedback and evidence; alert the teacher to problems.
THINK  Which task does a visitor recommendation add to our team’s work?
LIST TASKS OUR EVENT REALLY NEEDS
Our event / one visitor need to carry forward
Three real tasks / what finished work would look like

WORK CONNECTION  Ask the school event organiser how they check that a task has been accepted and completed. Record the person’s role, advice and date. Use an arranged school conversation rather than contacting strangers.
Organiser advice / date / how we will use it
THINK  Does every task in your chart have someone who accepts it?
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
AGREE ROLES AND CHECK UNDERSTANDING
150 minutes • Everyone takes a practical turn
1 TURN REQUIREMENTS INTO TASKS  |  20 MIN
Use the brief and visitor findings. Write each task on reused paper with its expected output. Consult the organiser about a real coordination difficulty.
2 AGREE FAIR RESPONSIBILITIES  |  25 MIN

Invite interests and learning goals. Give each student a meaningful task, a clear partner or backup and a chance to practise a new skill. Do not assign roles by gender, popularity, speed or who owns a device.
3 BUILD THE RESPONSIBILITY CHART  |  30 MIN
Complete page 100. Agree the owner, helper, deadline and checker for each task. Read back your responsibility in your own words. Record any teacher decision still needed.
4 TEST A REAL HANDOVER  |  35 MIN

Choose a small real task you can finish safely now, such as sorting visitor notes or drafting a task card. Work for 10 minutes, hand it to your backup, let them continue for 10 minutes and use the remaining 15 minutes to compare, clarify and revise. Record the test on page 101.
5 REVIEW THE WORKLOAD AND REVISE  |  20 MIN
Compare responsibilities. Move or split an overloaded task by agreement. Check that everyone has real work and that the backup understands it. Show the chart and test evidence to the teacher.
6 REFLECT AND RECEIVE FEEDBACK  |  20 MIN
Answer the five questions on page 102. Keep the first chart and revised chart, or mark dated revisions. Agree when the team will next check progress.
THINK  What would your backup need to know if you were absent at the next lesson?

SAFE BOUNDARIES  Adults handle electrical equipment, heavy lifting, money authorisation, crowd emergencies and first aid according to school arrangements. Students report concerns to the named teacher. A student role title never transfers adult responsibilities.
THINK  What did your backup actually manage to continue?

LOGBOOK 3  OUR RESPONSIBILITY CHART
An owner accepts the task • A checker verifies the output
TASK / OUTPUT
OWNER / HELPER
DEADLINE / CHECKER

Copy the sheet if needed. A helper is not an unnamed “everyone”. The checker may be a peer for a draft; the teacher retains required school approvals. Use school-approved storage and share student names only within the authorised class team.
THINK  Does our chart give someone a title without giving them a task they can actually perform?
My task / my first action / how I will show it is complete
My backup / what they need from me
A decision needing teacher approval / who will ask / by when
OUR TEAM AGREEMENT

□ We have explained our tasks back to each other. □ We will ask early when a deadline or task is unclear. □ We will record changes and share practical turns. □ We will listen to concerns and involve the teacher when needed.

TRY A HANDOVER AND IMPROVE IT
Use a real piece of work from your event
OUR SMALL TASK TEST
Task chosen / why it is safe and useful now
HANDOVER NOTE
OUR ACTUAL RECORD
Completed so far / evidence location
Next action / material needed
Deadline / unresolved question / person to ask

What the receiver actually continued
THINK  Did our partner continue the task successfully, or did we only give them a neat note?
MAKE ONE EVIDENCE BASED IMPROVEMENT
Confusion we observed / change to the handover or chart
Workload issue / agreed redistribution / date

GREEN AND DIGITAL PRACTICE  Reuse paper task cards and share existing tools. Keep one current chart, date revisions and store it where the team can access it safely. Do not post student contact details or team records publicly.
Next check date / who updates the shared chart
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 3  THINK AND REFLECT
Explain what you did and what improved
1 How did a requirement from the brief or visitor inquiry become a specific task?
2 What did your backup actually continue during the handover test?
3 Which responsibility was unclear or uneven, and how did the team change it?
4 How did you listen, include another person or resolve a disagreement?
5 How could a clear task and handover help when organising something at home?
WHAT DID WE LEARN

A working team needs accepted tasks, clear outputs and useful checks. A handover test reveals missing information. Shared records and fair practical turns help the team continue when plans or people change.
EVIDENCE OF LEARNING
□ Task cards linked to requirements  □ Responsibility chart and revisions □ Organiser advice  □ Actual handover work and receiver feedback □ Individual contribution  □ Reflection and teacher feedback
TEACHER FEEDBACK
I = independently; P = with a prompt; N = needs practice. Observe each student carrying out and handing over work.
AREA
OBSERVABLE EVIDENCE
I / P / N
Practical
Records an accepted task and gives a usable handover.
Work
Uses organiser advice and checks outputs and deadlines.
Values
Shares work fairly and responds constructively to feedback.
Home
Explains a realistic use for task sharing at home.
NEXT  Activity 4 — Design the Visitor Experience. Use the brief, visitor requirements and agreed responsibilities.
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 4  DESIGN THE VISITOR EXPERIENCE
Observe the venue • Make a layout • Test the journey
AI-generated illustrative photograph. Measure and record your own school venue; this is not its layout.
THINK  Could a first-time visitor find where to go without someone explaining every turn?
OUR LEARNING OBJECTIVE
We will turn visitor needs into an evidence-based venue layout, test a visitor journey and revise the plan after feedback.
TIME AND WHAT YOU NEED

180 instructional minutes. Bring the brief on page 87, visitor recommendations on page 95, team chart on page 100, reused paper, pencil, ruler and a shared measuring tape. Use existing tables or paper markers only with teacher permission. No device or purchase is required.
LET US UNDERSTAND

A visitor experience includes arriving, finding help, taking part and leaving. A layout shows where these actions can happen. It must fit the real venue and the school’s access and safety requirements. A neat drawing alone cannot show that a route works.

START HERE  Take the brief and visitor needs to the approved venue. Observe and measure before drawing positions. CHECK BEFORE MOVING ON  Your tester can try the route; keep the first plan and record the change and recheck.
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
EXPLORE THE REAL VENUE
Listen to visitors • Check the space • Record uncertainty
START WITH WHAT IS ALREADY AGREED

Keep the event purpose, venue limits and responsibility chart. Carry forward at least two actual visitor needs. Ask the organiser which doors, routes and areas must stay clear and which furniture students may measure or use.
LOOK OR ASK
RECORD FOR THE PLAN
Arrival and departure
Teacher-confirmed visitor entrance and exit route; signs or help needed.
Space and fixtures
Usable dimensions, fixed furniture, pillars and restricted areas.
Participation
Display positions, explanations and a place for approved seating or assistance.
Movement
Door swings, changes in level and places where people might stop or cross.
School arrangements
Adult-confirmed occupancy, emergency routes and required access checks.
THINK  Which feature looks usable on paper but still needs a real check with the school adult?
Two visitor needs / original visitor codes
Venue observation / measurement with unit / date
Organiser or caretaker role / advice / date

FIELDWORK CARE  Visit with the teacher. Keep doors and paths clear. Do not move heavy furniture, touch wiring, enter restricted spaces or decide room capacity from your own measurements. Record questions for the responsible adult.
THINK  Which proposed position still needs an adult check?
EVENT MANAGEMENT  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
BUILD AND TEST THE PLAN
180 minutes • Practical decisions supported by evidence
1 CHECK REQUIREMENTS  |  20 MIN
Read the brief and visitor recommendations. Agree the visitor journey and divide observation, measuring, drawing and checking tasks. Rotate roles so every student practises.
2 OBSERVE AND MEASURE  |  30 MIN
Walk the approved venue with the school adult. Record usable dimensions and fixed features. Measure from the same reference points, write units and recheck an important measurement with a partner.
3 DRAW THE FIRST LAYOUT  |  40 MIN

Use page 106 or an attached larger sheet. Mark fixed features first, then proposed displays, help desk, seating and movement. Use a simple scale only if dimensions are reliable; otherwise label the sketch “not to scale”. Add a key and version date.
4 TRY A VISITOR JOURNEY  |  40 MIN

Use a paper model or teacher-approved markers in the venue. A partner who did not draw the plan tries to find help, reach a display and leave. Observe actual hesitations and questions. Do not stage a crowd or block a real exit.
5 REVISE AND REVIEW  |  30 MIN
Use page 107 to connect each problem to an observed action and a change. Recheck the changed route. Show both versions to the teacher and record unresolved adult checks.
6 REFLECT AND DOCUMENT  |  20 MIN
Answer the five questions on page 108. Retain measurements, first and revised plans, route-test notes and individual contributions. Update the responsibility chart for the next task.
THINK  What could we observe during the trial that would show our layout needs a change?

ACCESS AND INCLUSION  Invite feedback about useful support without asking for medical details. Never simulate disability or ask someone to demonstrate difficulty. The teacher confirms suitable access arrangements and alternatives.
THINK  Where did the tester hesitate before your revision?
